title: 693. What’s Our Job as Humans Anymore?
summary: It may just be being human. Stephen Dubner interviews A.I. performer Tilly Norwood to find out if we are as replaceable as we fear. (Part two of a two-part series.)

title: 692. What Will A.I. Do to (and for) Human Creativity?
summary: Writers, designers, actors, coders, musicians, thinkers — they’re all worried about being replaced by machines. But what if the A.I.s are actually here to help? (Part one of a two-part series.)

title: Are Private Equity Firms Plundering the U.S. Economy? (Update)
summary: They say they make companies more efficient through savvy management. Critics say they bend the rules to enrich themselves at the expense of consumers and employees. Can they both be right? (Probably not.)

title: 691. Is This What a “Good Billionaire” Looks Like?
summary: David Rubenstein, a product of the old bipartisan D.C., made his fortune in private equity. He’s been spending it on “patriotic philanthropy” and institutions like the Kennedy Center, where Trump fired him as chairman. Now he wonders if the center can hold.

title: 690. It’s Show Business, Baby!
summary: Podcasting started as a niche-nerd pursuit. Now it’s a $9 billion industry. Is that a lot? The strange economics of this thing we do.

title: 689. Here’s Why Your Hamburger Just Got So Pricey
summary: An economist calls America’s beef industry a “miracle.” An antitrust scholar calls it “broken.” Maybe they’re both right?

title: 688. When Is a Bet Not a Bet?
summary: That’s the question at the heart of a battle between Kalshi and state gambling regulators. As prediction markets boom, there are other questions, too — about insider trading, market manipulation, and whether the public has turned against them. (Part two of a two-part series.)

title: 687. Are Prediction Markets the Best Forecasting Tool Ever — or Just Another Casino?
summary: The promise is that they can beat the experts at predicting inflation, elections, and FDA approvals. But right now, roughly 90 percent of the action is sports. Is this a future we want to bet on? Stephen Dubner speaks with, among others, the C.E.O. of Kalshi. (Part one of a two-part series.)

title: How to Be a Double Unicorn, with John Urschel | Better in Person
summary:
He was thriving in the N.F.L., but then he decided to focus on mathematics — a subject he now teaches at M.I.T. John walks Stephen Dubner through the whole story, teaches him some blocking techniques, and explains why some infinities are bigger than others.

If you'd like to see the video version of Better in Person, you can watch it on YouTube or Apple Podcasts.

title: 686. Why Is It So Hard to Find an NFL Quarterback?
summary: For decades, teams have tried (and mostly failed) to predict which college quarterbacks will thrive in the pros. Is the science finally catching up? Stephen Dubner speaks with a scout, a psychologist, a data warrior, and a Hall of Fame quarterback who nobody wanted.

title: Amazon Was Supposed to Kill the Bookstore. James Daunt Had Other Plans | Better in Person
summary:
He started with one small shop in London. He has since resuscitated both Barnes & Noble and Waterstones. He tells Stephen Dubner exactly how he does it.

If you'd like to see the video version of Better in Person, you can watch it on YouTube or Apple Podcasts.

title: 685. How to Survive the A.I. Shock
summary: Gina Raimondo, a former commerce secretary and governor, thinks A.I. will create plenty of jobs in the long run. She also thinks a poorly managed transition could tear the country apart. So she came up with a plan.

title: How to Run an Institution in an Anti-Institution Era | Better in Person
summary:
Anne Pasternak (Brooklyn Museum) and Michael Roth (Wesleyan University) tell Stephen Dubner how they keep the peace in the middle of a culture war.

If you'd like to see the video version of Better in Person, you can watch it on YouTube or Apple Podcasts.

title: How to Return Stolen Art (Update)
summary: Museums are purging their collections of looted treasures. Can they also get something in return? And what does it mean to be a museum in the 21st century? (Part 3 of an updated series originally published in 2023.)

title: “I Trust Almost Anyone More Than Myself” | Better in Person
summary:
The Pulitzer Prize-winning novelist Jennifer Egan talks about confidence, luck, and why it takes 35 drafts to get to the finish line.

If you'd like to see the video version of Better in Person, you can watch it on YouTube or Apple Podcasts.

title: Is a Museum Just a Trophy Case? (Update)
summary: The world’s great museums are full of art and artifacts that were plundered during an era when plunder was the norm. Now there’s a push to return these works to their rightful owners. Sounds simple, right? It's not. (Part 2 of an updated series originally published in 2023.)

title: Meet Warren Zanes, the Author and Rocker Behind the Springsteen Movie | Better in Person
summary:
When he joined the Del Fuegos, his big brother’s band, all Warren knew how to play was a record player. Things went great for a while — and then it all fell apart. So how did he wind up writing definitive books on Springsteen and Tom Petty? 

If you'd like to see the video version of Better in Person, you can watch it on YouTube or Apple Podcasts.

title: The Case of the $4 Million Gold Coffin (Update)
summary: How did a freshly looted Egyptian antiquity end up in the Metropolitan Museum of Art? Why did it take Kim Kardashian to crack the case? And how much of what you see in any museum is stolen? (Part 1 of “Stealing Art Is Easy. Giving It Back Is Hard,” first published in 2023.)

title: What if Being a Stranger Is Actually Your Superpower? | Better in Person
summary:
Angela Buchdahl was the first Asian American to be ordained as a rabbi, and now she is among the most influential rabbis in the world. She and Stephen Dubner talk about boundary-crossing, the aftermath of October 7, and whether you can be a good Jew without believing in God. 

If you'd like to see the video version of Better in Person, you can watch it on YouTube or Apple Podcasts.

title: 684. He Helped Clean Up the Last Crash. Does He See Another One Coming?
summary: Former S.E.C. chair Gary Gensler has had a front-row seat to numerous financial booms and busts. How does he feel about America’s massive bet on A.I.? “Something has to give.”

title: Does it Take a Twisted Mind to Write Twisted Stories? | Better In Person
summary:
Harlan Coben doesn’t think so. The mega-best-selling author talks suburbia, impostor syndrome, and what he learned from his college friend David Foster Wallace.

If you'd like to see the video version of Better in Person, you can watch it on YouTube or Apple Podcasts.

title: 683. In the New Space Race, Who Makes the Rules?
summary: Governments started the space age. Now, billionaires and private firms are reinventing it. Guest host Steve Levitt explores what the past can teach us about a high-stakes future. (Part two of a two-part series.)

title: How Gary Gulman Turned Depression Into Comedy Gold | Better in Person
summary:
Gary and Stephen talk about creativity, recovery, getting fired, and holding grudges. They also get outside and play basketball, which is a big part of how Gary stays well.

If you'd like to see the video version of Better in Person, watch it on YouTube or Apple Podcasts.

title: 682. Should A.I. Move to Space?
summary: At first it sounds ridiculous. But it might be inevitable. Guest host Steve Levitt talks to a team that hopes to push A.I. infrastructure off the planet. (Part one of a two-part series.)

title: Why Cooking is Caregiving, with Chef Hillary Sterling | Better in Person
summary:
Hillary Sterling was a Brooklyn kid raised on cream cheese sandwiches and canned potatoes. So how did she become one of New York City's best chefs? The Ci Siamo executive chef explains on the second episode of Better in Person. 

If you'd like to see the video version of Better in Person, watch it on YouTube or Apple Podcasts.

title: Are You Really Allergic to Penicillin? (Update)
summary: Like tens of millions of people, Stephen Dubner thought he had a penicillin allergy. Like the vast majority, he didn’t. This misdiagnosis costs billions of dollars and causes serious health problems, so why hasn’t it been fixed? We find out in this update of a 2025 episode.

title: How a Great Architect Thinks, with Bjarke Ingels | Better in Person
summary:
Is the oxymoron really “the secret sauce to everything”? That’s the case Ingels makes in this debut episode of our new video show Better in Person, filmed in Stephen Dubner’s living room.

If you'd like to see the video version of Better in Person, watch it on YouTube or Apple Podcasts.

title: 681. How to Host a Talk Show, with Dick Cavett
summary: Stephen Dubner had an idea for a new project. So he drove to Connecticut and knocked on the door of the master. Dubner’s new TV talk show Better in Person launches July 14 on the Freakonomics YouTube channel.

title: 680. Can Universities Win Back Our Trust?
summary: Dartmouth president Sian Beilock, a psychologist by training, made her name studying why people choke. Now she’s applying those insights to one of the most scrutinized jobs in America. No pressure!

title: 679. Why Does Vanderbilt Keep Winning?
summary: It’s a hard time to run a university: public trust is low, political pressure is high, and finances are fragile. But Daniel Diermeier, who trained as a political scientist, has Vanderbilt humming. How? He says the key is choosing magnets over wedges.

title: The World Is (Still) Drowning in Sludge
summary: Insurance forms that make no sense. Subscriptions that can’t be cancelled. A never-ending blizzard of automated notifications. In this update of a 2025 episode, Stephen Dubner discovers where all this sludge comes from — and how much it’s costing us.

title: 678. Who Gets to Choose a “Good Death”?
summary: New York is the latest state to legalize medical aid in dying. Stephen Dubner speaks with the governor who signed the law, a Nobel Prize-winning economist, a death doula — and an ethicist who thinks the very idea is wrong.

title: 677. Can Backgammon Save Us from Ourselves?
summary: It brings strangers together. It teaches probability, strategy, and emotional control. It has even helped N.F.L. teams win the Super Bowl. Stephen Dubner explores why this ancient game is having a renaissance. (Part two of a series, “We Are All Gamers Now.”)

title: This Is Your Brain on Pollution (Update)
summary: As the Trump administration rolls back environmental regulations, we revisit a 2022 episode that explored the hidden cost of an invisible threat: air pollution.

title: 676. Has America Lost the Plot?
summary: Another war in the Middle East. A retreat from the international order. A presidency built on self-dealing and arbitrary power. It’s enough to make you think the U.S. is in a steep decline — but Fareed Zakaria thinks otherwise.

title: The Vanishing Mr. Feynman (Update)
summary: In his final years, Richard Feynman's curiosity took him to some surprising places. We hear from his companions on the trips he took — and one he wasn’t able to. (Part three of a three-part series originally published in 2024.)

title: The Brilliant Mr. Feynman (Update)
summary: What happens when an existentially depressed and recently widowed young physicist from Queens gets a fresh start in California? We follow Richard Feynman out west, to explore his long and extremely fruitful second act. (Part two of a three-part series originally published in 2024.)

title: The Curious Mr. Feynman (Update)
summary: From the Manhattan Project to the Challenger investigation, the physicist Richard Feynman loved to shoot down what he called “lousy ideas.” Today, the world is awash in lousy ideas — so maybe it’s time to get some more Feynman in our lives? (Part one of a three-part series originally published in 2024.)

title: 675. Has the New York Times Become a Games Company?
summary: Not exactly. But their runaway success with games like Wordle says something bigger about the way we live now. (Part one of a series, “We Are All Gamers Now.”)

title: 674. How Does a Composer Feel After the World Premiere?
summary: Great. Then depressed. Then great again. Stephen Dubner gets the full story from David Lang; we also hear from some fans, and the New York Philharmonic’s president. The math and the aftermath of “wealth of nations.” (Part two of a series.)

title: Was Adam Smith Really a Right-Winger? (Update)
summary: Economists and politicians have turned him into a mascot for free-market ideology. Some on the left say the right has badly misread him. In this updated replay of a 2022 episode, we hold a very Smithy tug of war.

title: 673. What Is Money?
summary: That’s what the Pulitzer Prize-winning composer David Lang wanted to learn. So he turned Adam Smith’s The Wealth of Nations into an oratorio. We tag along as Lang’s piece heads toward its world premiere with the New York Philharmonic. (Part one of a two-part series.)

title: 672.  What Makes Judy Faulkner Run?
summary: Epic Systems manages the electronic health records for hundreds of millions of people. This makes Faulkner a healthcare heavyweight and one of the most successful female entrepreneurs in history. So why haven’t we ever heard much from her? Stephen Dubner travels to Verona, Wisc., to explore the Faulknerverse.

title: Why Does Everyone Hate Rats? (Update)
summary: New York City’s mayor called them “public enemy number one.” History books say they caused the Black Death — although recent scientific evidence disputes that claim. In an updated episode from 2025, we ask: Is the rat a scapegoat? And what does our rat hatred say about us?

title: 671. Why Has There Been So Little Progress on Alzheimer’s Disease?
summary: One possibility: a leading hypothesis pursued by researchers (and funders) was built on science that now appears to be fraudulent. Stephen Dubner speaks with the scientist and the journalist who blew the whistle.

title: 670. Beeconomics 101
summary: How do beekeepers make a living? Why is there so much honey fraud? And why did billions of bees suddenly disappear? To find out, guest host Steve Levitt activates his hive mind.

title: Ten Myths About the U.S. Tax System (Update)
summary: Nearly everything that politicians say about taxes is at least half a lie. They are also dishonest when it comes to the national debt. In this update of an episode from 2025, Stephen Dubner finds one of the few people in Washington who is willing to tell the truth — and it’s even worse than you think.

title: 669. Why Is 95 Percent of the World’s Bourbon Made in Kentucky?
summary: Is it tradition … or protectionism? And what happens when the bourbon boom turns into a glut?

title: 668. Do Taylor Swift and Bad Bunny Have Blood on Their Hands?
summary: As one researcher told us: “We’ve engineered a world where the most distracting device ever made is also the one we use to listen to music in the car." A new study tries to measure the cost.

title: In a Driverless World, Who Loses and Who Wins?
summary: In blue cities across the country, unions and politicians want to ban self-driving cars. In this episode from the Search Engine podcast, PJ Vogt visits Boston to sort the facts from the propaganda. (Part two of a two-part series.)
